content: The dictyostelids are a group of cellular slime molds. Under conditions where food, typically bacteria, is abundant, they exist as individual amoebae that feed and divide normally. However, when the food supply is depleted, these amoebae aggregate to form a multicellular structure known as a pseudoplasmodium or slug. This slug is distinct from the gastropod mollusk also called a slug. The slug has a defined anterior and posterior, responds to environmental cues such as light and temperature gradients, and is capable of migration. Under appropriate conditions, the slug matures into a fruiting body. This structure consists of a stalk that supports one or more spore-containing balls. The spores are dormant cells encased in resistant cell walls, which germinate into new amoebae when food becomes available. In the genus Acytostelium, the stalk is composed of cellulose, whereas in other dictyostelids, the stalk is made of cells, often utilizing a significant proportion of the original amoebae. Most of these stalk cells die during the formation of the stalk. There is a clear correspondence between specific regions of the slug and the resulting parts of the fruiting body. The aggregation of amoebae typically occurs in converging streams. Amoebae move using filose pseudopodia and are attracted to chemical signals produced by other amoebae. In Dictyostelium, aggregation is mediated by cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), while other species use different signaling molecules. In Dictyostelium purpureum, aggregation is based on kinship rather than mere proximity. Dictyostelium has been extensively studied as a model organism in molecular biology and genetics, particularly for its relevance to cell communication, differentiation, and programmed cell death. The mechanism of aggregation in Dictyostelium relies on cAMP as a signaling molecule. A single cell, often the founder of the colony, begins secreting cAMP in response to stress. Neighboring cells detect this signal and respond in two ways: they move toward the source of the signal and secrete additional cAMP to amplify the signal. This creates a relay effect, propagating the signal throughout the local population of amoebae and directing their movement toward the area of highest cAMP concentration. Within an individual cell, the process involves the following steps: 1. cAMP binds to receptors on the cell membrane, activating a G-protein. 2. The G-protein stimulates adenylate cyclase, which produces more cAMP. 3. The newly synthesized cAMP diffuses out of the cell into the surrounding medium. 4. Internal cAMP deactivates the external cAMP receptor, creating a feedback loop. 5. A separate G-protein activates phospholipase C, leading to the production of inositol trisphosphate (IP3). 6. IP3 induces the release of calcium ions, which act on the cytoskeleton to extend pseudopodia. The internal cAMP concentration oscillates, causing the cell to exhibit periodic behavior. This oscillatory activity produces the striking spiral patterns observed in converging colonies, reminiscent of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction and cyclic cellular automata. The entire genome of Dictyostelium discoideum was published in Nature in 2005 by Ludwig Eichinger and colleagues. It contains approximately 12,500 genes distributed across six chromosomes. For comparison, the human genome has 20,000–25,000 genes on 46 chromosomes. The genome of Dictyostelium is rich in the nucleotides adenosine and thymidine (~77%), which influences codon usage to favor these nucleotides in the third position. Tandem repeats of trinucleotides are abundant in Dictyostelium, a feature that, in humans, is associated with trinucleotide repeat disorders. Dictyostelium was first discovered in a North Carolina forest in 1935. Initially classified as a lower fungus, it was later reclassified into various kingdoms, including Proctotista, Fungi, and Tubulomitochondrae. By the 1990s, the current classification was widely accepted. The genome of dictyostelids shares greater similarity with those of animals and plants than with fungi. Many genes involved in the development of multicellular organisms are thought to have originated from an organism similar to Dictyostelium.
